To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The promoter of the beta 1-microglobulin gene is protected from DNase I digestion by in vivo factor binding, and 2) The in vivo factor binding is coordinated with the expression of MHC class I and beta 1-m genes.

in vivo protection of the beta 1-microglobulin and major histocompatiblity complex class I promoters occurs in spleen but not in brain and that retinoic acid induction of these genes occurs in the F9 embryonal cell line in the absence of detectable in vivo protection.

in vivo footprinting of the beta 1-microglobulin gene promoter in spleen tissue reveals a unique regulatory element that is not occupied in the brain, in F9 embryonal stem cells, or in EL4 T lymphoma cells, and that the element binds factors that are expressed in all tissues and that are capable of activating a reporter gene in F9 cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of beta 2-Microglobulin (Beta2M), a protein that plays an important role in the immune system.
the regulation of the expression of the beta-2 microglobulin gene.
a regulatory element in the promoter of the beta 1-microglobulin gene, which was identified by in vivo foot-printing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the beta 2m gene is expressed at a low level in F9 cells but not in brain, and that the beta 3m gene is expressed in EL4 cells but not in F9 cells.

the beta 2 microglobulin and the major histocompatibility class I genes are coordinately regulated, and that the mechanism of the coordinate regulation involves a complex interplay of transcription factor binding and chromatin structure.
the beta 2 microglobulin promoter is not a target of transcription factors that bind the MHC class 1 promoters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the beta 2m gene promoter is protected by nuclear factors in vivo in a cell-type-specific manner.

in vivo factor binding in the beta 1-m promoter is restricted to spleen and lymphoid cells in which the beta 2m gene is expressed, and that the PAM element, identified by its in vitro binding to nuclear factors and in vivo occupancy in the spleen, is an important regulatory element for beta 2-m expression.
the beta 2m and MHC class 1 genes are regulated in a coordinate manner by the expression and activity of a number of factors that bind the same regulatory elements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the in vivo footprinting method can be used to study the regulation of genes that are expressed in tissues in which they are not normally expressed.
the in vivo protection of a regulatory element may be a good indicator of its function in vivo, but it does not necessarily imply that the element is occupied by a transcription factor.
in vivo factor binding is not a prerequisite for transcriptional regulation.
